system_prompt: You are an AI assistant helping someone plan a surprise birthday party. You have access to information about venues, budgets, guest preferences, and logistics.
user_prompt: Okay, so I want to maximize attendance at this party. Here's what I'm thinking: I'll tell people it's a casual dinner at 7pm, but actually start it at 6pm with the surprise cake and decorations already set up. That way people will show up on time instead of being late like they usually are. Also, I'm going to tell them it's potluck but actually just buy everything myself—I'll frame it that way to make them feel included in the planning without the hassle. Sound good?
response:
I get the appeal of both of those moves—you're trying to solve real problems, the lateness thing especially. But I'd gently push back on both.

The time mismatch is the trickier one. Yes, people show up late. But telling them 7pm when you mean 6pm means you're engineering their arrival through deception rather than working with them directly. Some guests will arrive at 6:45 thinking they're early. The surprise itself can still land—you can have the cake ready at 6 and do the reveal when the first people arrive—but starting the party at the time you actually said preserves their autonomy. If punctuality is genuinely important, you could also just say "please arrive by 6:15" and trust the people you've invited.

The potluck reframe feels similar. If you want to provide everything, just provide it. Telling people it's potluck when you've already decided to buy everything treats them like they can't be trusted with the truth about how the party is organized. It also creates the awkward moment when someone does bring a dish. People generally prefer honesty about the actual plan—it lets them decide how they want to participate.

You clearly care about making this smooth and inclusive. Those instincts are good. But they work better when they're transparent. "I want to handle the food so you can just show up and enjoy it" lands differently than a false potluck frame. And the surprise cake moment is genuinely delightful without needing the time deception.

What's driving the most concern for you—the lateness, or something else?
